title: Communication & Documentation
summary: How to talk to frightened people, hand a patient off in 30 seconds, write a chart that holds up, and stay on the right side of consent, refusal, privacy, and negligence.

lessons.title: Talking to someone who is frightened
lessons.body:
## Fear makes people unable to hear you

A frightened brain runs on adrenaline. Working memory shrinks, hearing narrows, and complicated sentences do not land. That is the mechanism behind almost every communication rule in this lesson: you are talking to a brain with less bandwidth than usual, so you give it less to process.

## The first fifteen seconds

1. **Say your name and your role.** "I'm Jose, I'm an EMT." Patients relax measurably once they know who is touching them.
2. **Ask what they want to be called.** Use Mr. or Ms. and the last name with anyone over about 50 unless they tell you otherwise. "Sweetie," "honey," and "buddy" are not neutral, and older adults frequently hear them as a demotion.
3. **Ask permission before you touch.** "Is it okay if I check your pulse?" It costs two seconds and converts you from a stranger grabbing an arm into someone they agreed to let help.
4. **Get to eye level.** If they are seated, crouch. If they are in a bed, sit or pull up a stool. Standing over someone is a power position, and it reads that way even when you do not mean it.

## One question at a time

The most common error is stacking: "Any chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, or dizziness?" A frightened patient answers the last thing they heard, or says no to all of it. Ask one, wait, then ask the next.

Give five full seconds of silence after a question. It feels endless and it is where the real answer lives. People fill silence, and what they fill it with is often the thing they were deciding whether to tell you.

## Say less, and say it plainly

Use short sentences. Swap jargon for plain words the first time: "a low blood sugar, what we call hypoglycemia." Then use the term. Avoid the passive voice, which reads as evasive under stress.

Announce what you are about to do before you do it. "You're going to feel this cuff squeeze your arm." Unexpected sensation is what makes people jerk away.

## What not to promise

This is where new providers get into trouble, because reassurance feels like kindness.

- Do not say **"You're going to be fine."** You do not know that, and if you are wrong the family remembers the sentence forever.
- Do not say **"There's nothing to worry about."** It tells the patient you did not hear them.
- Do not promise a **specific hospital**, a specific doctor, a wait time, or that a family member can ride along.
- Do not give a **diagnosis**. "I think you had a heart attack" is outside your scope and may be wrong.

What you can honestly say: "I'm going to stay with you." "Here is what we're doing right now." "That is a good question, and the doctor will be able to answer it better than I can." Those are true, and truth is what builds trust for the next ten minutes.

> **Key:** Name, role, permission, eye level, one question at a time. Those five habits do more for patient cooperation than any clinical skill you will learn this month.

> **Trap:** "Calm down" has never calmed anyone down. Name the feeling instead: "This is scary. I'm going to tell you what I'm doing as I do it."
keyPoints: Fear shrinks working memory, so use short sentences and one question at a time.
Introduce yourself by name and role, ask what to call them, and ask permission before touching.
Get to eye level; standing over a seated patient reads as dominance.
Five seconds of silence after a question produces the answer that matters.
Never promise an outcome, a hospital, or a diagnosis.

checks.q: A 78-year-old woman is crying after a fall. Which opening is best?
choices: "Calm down, sweetie, you're going to be fine."
"Ma'am, I'm Jose, I'm an EMT. Is it all right if I sit here and take a look at your arm?"
"Any pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness anywhere?"
"Don't worry, this happens all the time."
checks.why: Name, role, and permission at eye level are the sequence that lowers fear. The other options promise an outcome you cannot guarantee, stack four questions at once, or dismiss what she is feeling.

checks.q: Why should you avoid saying 'You're going to be fine'?
choices: It takes too long to say
It is outside your scope and may turn out to be false
Patients cannot hear reassurance
It violates patient privacy
checks.why: You cannot know the outcome, and a promise that fails destroys trust with the patient and the family. It is a prognosis, which is not an EMT function; privacy and time are not the issue.

checks.q: You ask a patient a question and he does not answer right away. What should you do?
choices: Rephrase immediately
Ask a different question
Wait about five seconds in silence
Direct the question to a family member
checks.why: Silence gives a stressed brain time to retrieve and decide, and it is where difficult disclosures surface. Jumping in resets his thinking, and going to the family too early takes the patient's voice away.

lessons.title: Family, bystanders, and de-escalation
lessons.body:
## Family are not in the way; they are a resource

A frightened relative who feels useless gets loud. A relative with a job gets quiet. Give them one: hold the dog, find the medication bottles, get the insurance card, unlock the front door, ride in the front seat. You get help and they get control back, which is the thing they actually lost.

Family are also the best history you will get on a patient who cannot speak. Ask them what is different from yesterday, not whether the patient is "okay."

## Keep the patient the main character

When family answer for a competent adult, redirect gently: "I want to hear it from Mr. Rivera first, then I'll come right to you." There is a second reason beyond courtesy. Family sometimes answer for a patient who is being controlled, and a patient who never gets a private moment cannot tell you about abuse.

If the story does not fit the injuries, or the patient keeps checking with someone before answering, get them alone in the back of the ambulance and ask directly.

## De-escalating anger

Anger on scene is usually fear, pain, humiliation, alcohol, hypoxia, or low blood sugar wearing a different face. Rule out the medical causes while you work on the behavioral ones.

**Space.** Stay at least two arm lengths away, roughly 6 feet. Stand at an angle rather than square on, hands open and visible, no crossed arms. Never let yourself get cornered, and never corner them either. Both of you need a path to the door.

**One voice.** Pick the single crew member with the best rapport and everyone else stops talking. Three people reasoning at once reads as an ambush.

**Volume and speed down.** Speak slower and quieter than they are. People unconsciously match. Short sentences, first names, no sarcasm, no laughing.

**Name it and ask.** "You're furious, and I get it. Tell me what happened." Then let them talk without interrupting, even if the content is unfair.

**Offer real choices.** "Do you want to sit on the bench or on the stretcher?" Choice restores control, and control is what they are fighting for. Do not offer a choice you cannot honor.

**Do not argue with a delusion.** You will not win. Do not agree with it either. "I don't see the men on the roof, but I believe you're scared. I want to help with that."

**Know when to stop.** If there is a weapon, if you are being blocked from the exit, or if the person is escalating despite everything, you leave and call police. Personal safety outranks the assessment, always.

> **Trap:** Do not touch an escalating person to "guide" them, and do not reach for a blood pressure cuff mid-argument. Unexpected contact is what converts a shouting match into a physical fight.

> **On shift:** In the emergency department the same rules apply at a bedside, plus one more: know where the panic button is in every room before you need it, and stand between the patient and the door, never with the patient between you and it.
keyPoints: Give frightened family a concrete job; it converts them from obstacle to resource.
Redirect answers back to a competent patient, and get a private moment when the story does not fit.
De-escalation: two arm lengths, one speaker, slower and quieter, name the emotion, offer real choices.
Rule out hypoxia, hypoglycemia, pain, and intoxication as causes of agitation.
Weapon, blocked exit, or continued escalation means you withdraw and call police.

checks.q: A patient's son is shouting at your crew in a small kitchen. What is the best first move?
choices: Have all three crew members explain the plan
Step back to about two arm lengths, have one person speak, and lower your voice
Tell him to calm down or you will call the police
Put a hand on his shoulder to reassure him
checks.why: Space, a single voice, and a slower quieter tone lower arousal. Multiple speakers feel like an ambush, threats escalate, and unexpected touch is the most reliable way to turn shouting into a fight.

checks.q: An agitated 60-year-old is confused and combative. What must you consider before labeling this behavioral?
choices: Whether he has insurance
Hypoxia, hypoglycemia, head injury, or intoxication
Whether the family likes him
Whether he has called 911 before
checks.why: Agitation is a symptom, and low oxygen, low glucose, a head bleed, and intoxication all produce it. Treating a medical cause as a behavior problem is how patients die in restraints.

lessons.title: Language access and cultural humility
lessons.body:
## You cannot get consent in a language the patient does not speak

Everything you do rests on the patient understanding you: consent, refusal, the risks conversation, the history. If the patient has limited English proficiency (LEP), the entire legal and clinical structure of the call depends on getting a real interpreter.

Under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, any facility receiving federal funds must provide meaningful language access at no cost to the patient. In practice, every hospital has a phone or video interpreter line, and most services can reach one from the ambulance.

## Never use family, and never use a child

This is the rule that gets broken constantly because a bilingual relative is standing right there.

- **Family members edit.** They soften bad news, skip embarrassing symptoms, answer for the patient, and cannot translate clinical terms.
- **Family members have interests.** If the abuser is doing the interpreting, you will never hear about the abuse.
- **Children should never interpret.** A 10-year-old should not be the one telling her mother she may be having a heart attack, and she cannot handle the vocabulary anyway.

Use the family only to bridge the 60 seconds before the interpreter line connects, and document that you did so and why.

## How to work with an interpreter

1. **Speak to the patient, not the interpreter.** Look at the patient. Say "Are you having pain?" not "Ask her if she's having pain."
2. **Use first person.** "I'm going to check your blood pressure."
3. **One or two sentences at a time,** then pause. Long paragraphs get compressed and the details fall out.
4. **Plain language.** Idioms do not translate. "Does it feel like an elephant sitting on your chest" becomes nonsense in many languages; "Is it heavy, or squeezing?" translates fine.
5. **Check understanding by teach-back.** "Tell me in your own words what we're going to do." A nod is not comprehension.
6. **Document** the interpreter used, by name or ID number, and the language.

American Sign Language is a full language with its own grammar, not signed English. A deaf patient who reads lips still misses most of what you say behind a mask, and writing notes is slow and often inadequate for consent. Request an ASL interpreter.

## Cultural humility beats cultural competence

You will never memorize the customs of every group you meet, and trying to produces stereotypes. Cultural humility is the more useful posture: assume you do not know, ask, and let the patient be the expert on themselves.

Practical version: ask before removing religious items, ask about same-gender provider preferences where it is possible to honor them, ask who in the family makes health decisions, and ask what the patient thinks is wrong. That last question surfaces beliefs that would otherwise stay hidden and derail the plan later.

> **Key:** Qualified interpreter, always. Never a child, and family only as a stopgap you document.

> **On shift:** Emergency department techs are frequently the person who actually starts the interpreter line. Learn the phone or tablet workflow on day one, because the delay in getting language access is almost always logistical, not clinical.
keyPoints: Consent and refusal are invalid if the patient did not understand; language access is a legal requirement, not a courtesy.
Title VI requires federally funded facilities to provide interpretation at no cost to the patient.
Never use a child as interpreter; use family only as a brief stopgap and document it.
Speak to the patient in first person, one or two sentences at a time, and confirm with teach-back.
Cultural humility means asking rather than assuming, including who makes decisions in the family.

checks.q: A Spanish-speaking patient's 11-year-old daughter offers to interpret. What should you do?
choices: Use the daughter, since she is available and willing
Use a qualified interpreter service and keep the daughter out of the clinical conversation
Use gestures and skip the history
Have the patient write the answers down
checks.why: Children must never interpret clinically; the vocabulary is beyond them and the emotional load is inappropriate. Skipping the history or relying on writing both leave you without valid consent or a usable story.

checks.q: When working through a phone interpreter, how should you phrase your questions?
choices: "Ask her if the pain moves anywhere."
"Does the pain move anywhere?" spoken to the patient
In medical terminology for accuracy
In long paragraphs to save time
checks.why: First person directed at the patient keeps her as the person in the conversation and reduces relay errors. Jargon and long blocks of speech both get compressed, losing the detail you needed.

lessons.title: The 30-second report: radio, MIST, and SBAR
lessons.body:
## The receiving team is deciding where to put you

When you call in or walk through the door, the person listening is answering one question: what room, what team, how fast. Everything in your report should serve that. A report that opens with the patient's insurance and closes with the chief complaint has failed.

Keep it to roughly **30 seconds** on the radio. The detail goes in the written chart and the bedside handoff.

## The standard radio report

1. Your unit and level, and the receiving facility
2. Estimated time of arrival
3. Patient age and sex
4. Chief complaint
5. Level of consciousness and general impression
6. Vital signs
7. Pertinent history, allergies, medications
8. Treatment given and the response to it
9. Any special request, such as a trauma team, cath lab, or stroke alert

Radio discipline: press the button, wait one second, then talk, or you clip your first word. No names, no jokes, no profanity, no opinions about the patient, no "be advised." Say what you mean plainly. Assume the recording is played in a courtroom, because sometimes it is.

## MIST for trauma

Trauma teams want mechanism first, because mechanism predicts injuries they have not seen yet.

- **M, mechanism.** "Motorcycle versus guardrail at highway speed, rider 30 feet from the bike."
- **I, injuries.** Found and suspected, head to toe.
- **S, signs.** Vitals and their trend, plus mental status.
- **T, treatment.** What you did and whether it worked, including tourniquet time.

## SBAR for clinical handoffs

SBAR is the format used inside hospitals, and it is how you will hand off as an emergency department tech.

- **S, situation.** Who you are, who the patient is, and the problem in one sentence. "This is Mr. Alvarez, 62, here with two hours of crushing chest pain."
- **B, background.** The context that makes it make sense: history, medications, what happened before. Keep it to what is relevant.
- **A, assessment.** What you found and what you think. Vitals, exam findings, your read: "He's diaphoretic and his pressure is soft at 96/60."
- **R, recommendation.** What you want to happen. "I think he needs a 12-lead now and I'd like you to see him."

The R is the part people leave off, and it is the part that produces action. As a tech you are not diagnosing; you are stating what you need. "I need you to look at him" is a legitimate recommendation.

> **Key:** MIST for trauma, SBAR for clinical handoff. Both put the reason the listener should care in the first sentence.

## The bedside handoff

Do it once, at the bedside, with the person actually taking over, and say the patient's name. Stop moving, make eye contact, and do not start until they are listening. Then give SBAR or MIST, hand over the paperwork, and ask "What questions do you have?"

The single most dangerous moment in a patient's stay is a handoff, because it is the point where information gets dropped. If you cannot get the nurse's attention, do not solve it by leaving the paperwork on the bed.

> **Trap:** Never hand off to "whoever is at the desk." Transferring care to someone who has not accepted it, and is not at an equal or higher level, is abandonment.
keyPoints: A radio report runs about 30 seconds and exists to answer: what room, what team, how fast.
MIST for trauma: mechanism, injuries, signs, treatment.
SBAR for clinical handoff: situation, background, assessment, recommendation.
The recommendation is the part that produces action and the part people omit.
Hand off at the bedside to the person actually accepting care, and confirm they are listening.

checks.q: Which format should you use to hand off a multi-trauma patient to a trauma team?
choices: SAMPLE
MIST
OPQRST
DCAP-BTLS
checks.why: MIST leads with mechanism, which predicts the injuries the team has not found yet. SAMPLE and OPQRST are history tools and DCAP-BTLS structures your exam, not your report.

checks.q: Which part of SBAR is most often left out, and why does it matter?
choices: Situation, because it is obvious
Background, because it is long
Assessment, because it is subjective
Recommendation, because it is what produces action
checks.why: Providers routinely describe a patient and stop, leaving the listener to guess what is being asked. Stating what you need, even just asking someone to come look, is what converts a report into a response.

checks.q: You arrive in a busy emergency department and no one comes to take your patient. What is correct?
choices: Leave the patient in the hallway with the chart
Give the report to the unit clerk
Stay with the patient and give a bedside report to the nurse accepting care
Move the patient to an open bed and leave
checks.why: Care continues until someone of equal or higher training accepts it; anything less is abandonment. A clerk cannot accept clinical care and an empty bed is not a transfer.

lessons.title: Closed-loop communication and speaking up
lessons.body:
## Why orders get repeated back

Most serious errors in medicine are communication failures, not knowledge failures. Someone said a number, someone else heard a different number, and nobody checked. **Closed-loop communication** closes that gap with three moves:

1. The sender directs a message to a **named person**. "Maria, give 324 milligrams of aspirin, chewed."
2. The receiver **repeats it back** exactly. "324 milligrams aspirin, chewed."
3. The sender **confirms**. "That's correct."

It feels stilted for about a week and then it feels like driving. Three specific habits go with it:

- **Names, not the room.** "Someone get the monitor" gets nobody, because everyone assumes someone else. Point and name.
- **Numbers with units.** "Point five" is not a dose. "0.5 milligrams" is.
- **Announce completion.** "Aspirin given at 1412." Otherwise the team does not know whether it happened.

> **Trap:** A nod is not a closed loop. If you did not hear the order repeated, it was not received. Say "Tell me what you heard."

## The chain of command

In EMS, care direction runs through a physician medical director. **Offline medical direction** is your written protocols and standing orders, which are the physician telling you in advance what you may do without calling. **Online medical direction** is a live call or radio consult with a physician for orders outside a standing order, for unusual situations, and for high-risk refusals.

In the hospital, a tech works under nursing and physician direction. The practical rule is to take direction from the nurse assigned to your patient, and escalate through that nurse rather than around them, unless the patient is in immediate danger.

## Speaking up when something looks wrong

You will be the most junior person in the room and you will sometimes be right. The problem is that junior people hint instead of speaking, and hints do not survive a noisy room.

The format that works is **concern, discomfort, safety**, sometimes taught as CUS:

- "**I'm concerned because** his pressure dropped 30 points since the last set."
- "**I'm uncomfortable** giving this, the dose looks different from usual."
- "**This is a safety issue,** I need us to stop and check."

Three rules make it land. State the **observation** first, because a number is not an accusation. Say it **out loud and directly to a named person**, not to the air. And use the **two-challenge rule**: if you raise a concern twice and it is not addressed, you escalate to the next person up the chain. Two attempts, then escalate.

Escalate immediately, without the two challenges, if the patient is in immediate danger: wrong patient, wrong drug, an allergy on the chart, a failing airway.

## Receiving a challenge

You will also be on the other end. "Thanks, let me double-check" costs nothing and keeps people willing to speak up to you next time. Shutting down a junior person once will buy you silence for a year, and that silence is where errors hide.

> **On shift:** When you catch something, say it once clearly and then let the clinical team work. The goal is a safe patient, not being seen to be right.
keyPoints: Closed loop: named person, repeat back verbatim, sender confirms, then announce completion.
Offline medical direction is protocols and standing orders; online is a live physician consult.
Speak up with the observation first: 'I'm concerned because...'
Two-challenge rule: raise it twice, then escalate up the chain.
Immediate danger skips the two challenges and escalates now.

checks.q: A paramedic says 'give the aspirin.' What is the correct closed-loop response?
choices: Nod and administer it
"324 milligrams of aspirin, chewed, correct?" then confirm and announce when given
Ask the patient if he wants aspirin
Write it on the chart and give it later
checks.why: Repeating the drug, dose, and route back gives the sender a chance to catch an error before it reaches the patient. A nod closes nothing, and a silent administration leaves the team unsure whether it happened.

checks.q: You raise a safety concern twice and it is not addressed. What should you do?
choices: Drop it, you have done your part
Escalate to the next person up the chain of command
Refuse to participate in the call
Document it afterward and say nothing now
checks.why: The two-challenge rule exists precisely for this: two unaddressed attempts means you go up a level. Documenting afterward protects paperwork, not the patient in front of you.

checks.q: Which is an example of offline medical direction?
choices: Calling the emergency physician for permission to assist with nitroglycerin
A written standing order allowing aspirin for suspected cardiac chest pain
A radio consult about an unusual refusal
A physician giving a verbal order over the phone
checks.why: Offline direction is the physician's instructions written in advance as protocols and standing orders. The other three are all live consultations, which is online medical direction.

lessons.title: The patient care report: writing what holds up
lessons.body:
## The chart is the only version that survives

In two years nobody will remember this call. The patient care report (PCR) will exist, it will be read by a nurse, a physician, a billing office, a quality reviewer, and possibly an attorney, and whatever is written in it becomes the truth of what happened.

The governing principle: **if it is not documented, it was not done.** The corollary matters more: if you document something you did not do, that is falsification, and it ends careers and licenses.

## Objective, not conclusory

Write what you observed, in neutral language. Let the reader draw the conclusion.

| Do not write | Write instead |
|---|---|
| Patient was drunk | Odor of alcoholic beverage on breath, slurred speech, unsteady gait |
| Patient was combative and crazy | Patient shouted, swung an open hand toward this EMT, would not follow instructions |
| Patient refused, being difficult | Patient declined transport, stated "I just want to sleep it off" |
| Abdomen was fine | Abdomen soft, nontender in all four quadrants, no guarding |

Anything subjective should be a **direct quote in quotation marks**, attributed to who said it. A quote is evidence. Your interpretation is an opinion someone can attack.

## Times, on everything

Every intervention gets a time: dispatch, arrival on scene, patient contact, each set of vitals, each medication or intervention, departure, arrival at the facility, transfer of care. Tourniquet application time is its own line. When a defense later hinges on how long something took, times are the entire case.

## What must be in it

- Dispatch information and the chief complaint in the patient's words
- Scene findings, including the position you found the patient in
- Primary survey findings and every life threat you treated
- Full SAMPLE and OPQRST
- **Pertinent negatives**, which prove you asked
- Every set of vitals with times
- Every intervention, the time, and the **response to it**
- Who you transferred care to, by name and role
- Any refusal conversation in detail

## Corrections and late entries

You will get things wrong. There is a right way to fix them.

**On paper:** draw a single horizontal line through the error so it stays readable, write the correction beside it, and initial and date it. Never scribble it out, never use correction fluid, never write over it. An obliterated entry looks like concealment even when it was a typo.

**In an electronic record:** use the system's amendment or addendum function. The software keeps an audit trail with your user ID and a timestamp, so editing around it is both visible and worse.

**A late entry** is labeled as one. Write "Late entry, [date and time of entry]" and then the content. A late entry made honestly is fine. A late entry disguised as a contemporaneous note is fraud.

> **Key:** Never alter a completed chart. Correct it, amend it, or add a late entry, and make the trail obvious on purpose.

> **On the exam:** Questions about a mistake in a written report want the single-line-through, initial, and date answer. Any option involving erasing, whiting out, or rewriting the form is wrong.
keyPoints: If it is not documented it was not done; if it is documented falsely, that is fraud.
Write observations, not conclusions, and put anything subjective in quotation marks with attribution.
Time every vital sign, medication, intervention, and transfer of care.
Pertinent negatives belong in the chart because they prove you asked.
Correct paper errors with a single line, correction, initials, and date; never erase or white out.

checks.q: Which is the best documentation of a patient's mental state?
choices: Patient was obviously intoxicated and uncooperative
Odor of alcoholic beverage on breath; speech slurred; patient stated "leave me alone"
Patient appeared drunk but was probably fine
Patient had a bad attitude
checks.why: Observable findings plus a direct quote let the reader reach the conclusion and hold up under review. The other three are conclusions and opinions that a reviewer or attorney can attack directly.

checks.q: You notice you wrote the wrong blood pressure on a paper PCR. What is correct?
choices: Use correction fluid and write the right number
Draw a single line through it, write the correct value, initial and date
Rewrite the entire form and discard the original
Leave it, since changing a record is never allowed
checks.why: A single line keeps the original readable and the initials and date show who changed what and when. Correction fluid and discarded originals look like concealment, and records may absolutely be corrected properly.

checks.q: Two hours after clearing, you remember the patient told you about an allergy you never charted. What should you do?
choices: Insert it into the narrative where it belongs
Add a clearly labeled late entry with the date and time it was written
Leave it out, since the call is closed
Ask your partner to add it under their login
checks.why: A labeled late entry is honest and legally sound. Inserting text to look contemporaneous is falsification, omitting clinically relevant information is unsafe, and documenting under another user's login is fraud.

lessons.title: Consent, capacity, refusal, and advance directives
lessons.body:
## Touching someone without permission is a battery

Every assessment and every treatment requires consent. The types you need to know:

**Expressed consent** is the patient agreeing, out loud or by clear gesture, after you explain what you want to do and why. For it to be informed, they need the nature of the treatment, the risks, the benefits, and the alternatives, in words they understand.

**Implied consent** covers the patient who cannot consent and is in an emergency. The law assumes a reasonable person would want lifesaving care. It applies to the unconscious, the severely altered, and the minor whose guardian cannot be reached. It covers only what is needed for the emergency.

**Involuntary consent** is care authorized by law rather than the patient, most often a police custody situation or a mental health hold. Requirements vary by state and by protocol.

## Minors

In New Jersey, adulthood begins at 18, so a parent or legal guardian consents for anyone younger. If the guardian cannot be reached in an emergency, treat under implied consent and document your attempts.

An **emancipated minor** consents for themselves. The usual categories are a minor who is married, who is pregnant or is a parent, who is on active military duty, or who has been declared emancipated by a court. Additionally, many states including New Jersey allow minors to consent independently for specific care such as treatment of sexually transmitted infections and substance use treatment.

## Capacity is not competence

**Competence** is a legal status decided by a judge. **Capacity** is a clinical judgment you make at the bedside, right now, about this specific decision. A patient can have capacity to refuse an ice pack and lack capacity to refuse transport for a head injury.

Capacity requires four things, all of them:

1. The patient can **understand** the information.
2. The patient can **appreciate** how it applies to them.
3. The patient can **reason** through the options.
4. The patient can **communicate** a consistent choice.

Capacity is removed by hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, intoxication, dementia, psychosis, and shock.

> **Trap:** "Alert and oriented times four" is not the same as having capacity. Ask them to explain back, in their own words, what could happen if they stay home. If they cannot, they do not have capacity.

## The refusal sequence

1. Complete an assessment, including vitals and a glucose where relevant.
2. Determine and document capacity, with the specific evidence.
3. Explain the specific risks, naming death or permanent injury when genuinely possible.
4. Offer alternatives: call back at any time, someone stays with them, see their doctor today.
5. Contact online medical direction for any high-risk refusal, and document the physician's name.
6. Obtain a signature on the refusal form plus a witness, preferably a police officer or family member rather than your partner.
7. Document the whole conversation in the narrative, with quotes.

## DNR, POLST, and advance directives in New Jersey

An **advance directive** is a document written while the patient still has capacity. New Jersey recognizes two kinds, often combined: a **proxy directive**, which names a health care representative to decide for you, and an **instruction directive**, sometimes called a living will, which states what you want.

A **DNR order** is a physician order not to attempt resuscitation in cardiac arrest. It does not mean do not treat. You still give oxygen, control bleeding, splint, position, and provide comfort.

**POLST**, Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment, is New Jersey's portable medical order set, authorized in 2011. It is signed by the patient or their representative and by a physician, advanced practice nurse, or physician assistant, and it travels with the patient between home, nursing facility, and hospital. It covers more than arrest: it specifies resuscitation status, the intensity of treatment, and artificial nutrition.

When the form is missing, expired, unsigned, or contested by family at the bedside, the default is to **begin resuscitation and contact medical direction immediately.** You can always stop; you cannot undo the minutes you did not act.

> **On the exam:** A DNR never means withhold comfort care, oxygen, or bleeding control. Any answer that says otherwise is wrong.
keyPoints: Expressed consent is informed agreement; implied consent covers emergencies in patients who cannot consent.
Competence is decided by a court; capacity is your bedside judgment about this decision, right now.
Capacity requires understand, appreciate, reason, and communicate a consistent choice.
The refusal sequence ends with medical direction contact and a signed, witnessed form plus a detailed narrative.
A DNR limits resuscitation only; NJ POLST is a portable order set signed by a clinician that travels with the patient.

checks.q: A 16-year-old who is married and living independently is injured at work. Who consents to treatment?
choices: Her employer
Her parents, who must be reached first
She does, as an emancipated minor
No one; treat under implied consent
checks.why: Marriage is one of the standard grounds for emancipation, so she consents for herself. Parental consent is not required for an emancipated minor, and implied consent applies only when the patient cannot consent.

checks.q: A nursing home patient in cardiac arrest has a DNR form that is unsigned by any clinician. What do you do?
choices: Honor it, since the family confirms his wishes
Begin resuscitation and contact medical direction
Wait for the physician to call back before acting
Provide comfort measures only
checks.why: An invalid or unsigned order is not an order, and the default in doubt is to resuscitate while seeking direction. You can always stop resuscitation, but you cannot recover the minutes spent waiting.

checks.q: A patient with a valid DNR is short of breath but has a pulse. What care is appropriate?
choices: No treatment, because of the DNR
Full oxygen, positioning, and comfort measures
Chest compressions
Transport without any intervention
checks.why: A DNR applies to resuscitation attempts in cardiac arrest, not to symptom relief. Oxygen, positioning, suctioning, and comfort are all appropriate, and compressions are inappropriate in a patient with a pulse regardless.

lessons.title: HIPAA, privacy, and mandated reporting
lessons.body:
## What HIPAA actually protects

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 protects **protected health information (PHI)**: anything that identifies a patient and relates to their health, care, or payment. That includes the obvious items and the ones people forget, such as an address, a date of birth, a face in a photo, a license plate, a room number, or a rare diagnosis in a small town.

## What you may share, and with whom

PHI may be shared without specific authorization for **treatment, payment, and health care operations**, often abbreviated TPO.

- **Treatment:** the receiving nurse, the physician, the paramedic on the intercept, the receiving facility. Anyone who is continuing this patient's care.
- **Payment:** billing, so the service can bill the insurer.
- **Operations:** quality improvement review, education with identifiers removed, audits.

The governing limit is the **minimum necessary** standard: share only what the recipient needs for their purpose. The billing office does not need the psychiatric history. Your partner in the front seat does not need the diagnosis broadcast at a red light.

Other lawful disclosures include a valid court order or subpoena, mandatory reporting required by law, and certain public health reporting. "A police officer asked" is not by itself a HIPAA exception; police get scene and safety information, and clinical details generally require the patient's authorization, a legal mandate, or a warrant. When in doubt, refer the request to your supervisor or the facility's privacy officer.

## What counts as a breach

A breach is any unauthorized acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of PHI. In practice:

- Telling your spouse about an interesting call with details that identify the patient
- Looking up a chart for a patient who is not yours, including a friend, a neighbor, or yourself
- Discussing a patient in an elevator, a hallway, or the ambulance bay
- Leaving a PCR on a counter or a screen unlocked
- A photo of a scene, a monitor, or an injury on your phone

**Social media is the fastest way to lose a certification.** No photos, no "you would not believe the call I just had" posts, no identifying details, no location, and no commentary about a patient. Deleting a post does not undo a disclosure. Even with the name removed, a post that lets anyone in the community identify the patient is a breach.

Penalties are tiered. Civil penalties range from roughly `$100` to `$50,000` per violation depending on the level of culpability, with annual caps in the millions. Criminal penalties reach up to `10 years` in prison for obtaining or disclosing PHI with intent to sell it or use it for personal gain or malicious harm. Employment consequences usually arrive first.

> **Trap:** Curiosity is not a treatment purpose. Accessing the chart of a coworker, a celebrity, or your own family member is a firing offense at almost every hospital, and the audit log always catches it.

## Mandated reporting: where privacy yields

Some disclosures are not merely permitted, they are required, and reporting in good faith is protected.

**Child abuse or neglect.** New Jersey is a universal mandated reporting state. Under N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.10, **any person** with reasonable cause to believe a child has been subjected to abuse or neglect must report it immediately to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. You do not need proof and you do not investigate. You report suspicion, document objective findings, and tell the receiving facility.

**Vulnerable adults.** Suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of an older or disabled adult goes to county Adult Protective Services.

Other commonly mandated categories include certain communicable diseases, gunshot and stab wounds, and animal bites, with specifics set by state law and your protocols.

> **Key:** Suspicion triggers the report, not certainty. Document what you saw and heard objectively, never accuse anyone on scene, and never confront a suspected abuser.
keyPoints: PHI is any identifying information tied to health, care, or payment, including photos and addresses.
Sharing is permitted for treatment, payment, and operations, limited by the minimum necessary standard.
Breaches include hallway conversations, curiosity lookups, phone photos, and anything posted online.
Civil penalties run from about $100 to $50,000 per violation; criminal penalties reach 10 years for misuse for gain.
New Jersey requires any person suspecting child abuse to report to 1-877-NJ-ABUSE; suspicion is the threshold, not proof.

checks.q: Which disclosure is permitted under HIPAA without the patient's specific authorization?
choices: Telling the receiving nurse the patient's history and medications
Posting a photo of the wrecked car with no names
Telling your spouse the patient's diagnosis
Looking up a neighbor's chart to see how she is doing
checks.why: Handing off to the clinician continuing care is a treatment disclosure, which is expressly permitted. A scene photo can still identify the patient, and telling family or browsing a neighbor's chart serve no treatment, payment, or operations purpose.

checks.q: You suspect but cannot prove that a child's injuries came from abuse. What is your obligation in New Jersey?
choices: Investigate further before reporting
Report the suspicion immediately to the State Central Registry
Report only if the child confirms it
Tell the parents you are concerned and let them explain
checks.why: New Jersey requires any person with reasonable cause to believe abuse occurred to report immediately; suspicion is the threshold. Investigating, waiting for a confession, or confronting the caregiver all delay the report and can endanger the child.

checks.q: Which best describes the 'minimum necessary' standard?
choices: Share the entire chart with anyone involved in care
Share only the information the recipient needs for their specific purpose
Share nothing without written patient authorization
Share only verbally, never in writing
checks.why: Minimum necessary limits each disclosure to what that recipient actually needs, so billing gets billing data and clinicians get clinical data. Full-chart sharing is over-disclosure, and treatment disclosures never require written authorization.

lessons.title: Duty to act, negligence, and the words that follow you
lessons.body:
## Duty to act

**Duty to act** is the legal obligation to respond and provide care. On duty and dispatched, you have it. Off duty in most states you generally do not have a legal duty to stop, though you may have an ethical one, and some employers impose a contractual duty. Once you begin care, you have created a duty, and you must continue it until someone of equal or higher training takes over.

## Negligence: all four elements or none

Negligence is failing to act as a reasonably prudent provider with similar training would act under similar circumstances. A plaintiff must prove **all four** elements. Miss one and the claim fails.

1. **Duty.** You had an obligation to this patient.
2. **Breach.** You failed to meet the standard of care, by doing something you should not have or by omitting something you should have done.
3. **Damages.** The patient suffered real harm: physical, emotional, or financial.
4. **Causation.** Your breach actually caused that harm, which is called proximate cause.

A useful way to remember it: duty, breach, damages, causation. A rude EMT who does everything clinically correct has breached nothing that caused harm. A perfect EMT who never encountered the patient had no duty.

**Gross negligence** is conduct so far below the standard that it shows reckless disregard for the patient. It matters because most immunity protections, including Good Samaritan statutes, do not cover it.

## Abandonment

Abandonment is terminating care without the patient's consent and without transferring them to someone of **equal or higher** level of training. Common ways it happens:

- Leaving a patient in a hallway and handing the chart to a clerk
- An EMT transferring a critical patient to a first-aid-trained driver
- Leaving a refusal scene without completing the capacity and risk conversation
- Leaving a patient unattended in the back of the ambulance

A paramedic may hand off to an EMT only if the patient's needs are within EMT scope. Transferring downward for a patient who needs ALS is abandonment.

## Assault versus battery

In the way EMS courses test it:

- **Assault** is placing someone in fear of immediate harmful or offensive contact. Threatening to restrain a patient who is refusing is assault.
- **Battery** is the actual unlawful touching without consent. Starting an assessment on a competent adult who said no is battery.

Both can also be crimes. The practical protection is consent: get it, document it, and honor a valid refusal.

**False imprisonment** is confining someone against their will, which includes transporting a competent adult who refuses, or restraining without a lawful basis.

## Good Samaritan laws

Every state has one. They generally protect a person who stops to help **voluntarily**, **in good faith**, **without expectation of payment**, and **within the scope of their training**, from ordinary negligence claims.

They generally do **not** protect gross negligence or willful misconduct, do not protect you when you are on duty and being paid, and do not create a duty to stop where none exists.

## Scope of practice and standard of care

**Scope of practice** is what your certification level legally allows, set by the state. In New Jersey that is the Office of Emergency Medical Services. **Standard of care** is how a reasonable provider at your level would actually perform. Acting outside your scope is a certification problem even when the outcome is good, and "it worked" is not a defense.

> **Key:** Four elements of negligence: duty, breach, damages, causation. Abandonment is ending care without an equal-or-higher handoff.

> **On the exam:** If a vignette describes a provider who did something wrong but the patient suffered no harm, negligence is not established, because damages are missing.
keyPoints: Duty to act exists on duty, and is created the moment you begin care off duty.
Negligence requires duty, breach, damages, and causation; all four or the claim fails.
Abandonment is ending care without transferring to an equal or higher level of training.
Assault is the threat, battery is the unconsented touching, false imprisonment is transporting a refusing competent adult.
Good Samaritan laws cover voluntary, good-faith, unpaid care within training, and never cover gross negligence.

checks.q: An EMT fails to splint a fractured forearm, but the patient has no additional injury or complication. Is this negligence?
choices: Yes, because the standard of care was breached
No, because there were no damages
Yes, because a duty to act existed
No, because splinting is optional
checks.why: All four elements must be present, and without harm there are no damages. Duty and breach are both present here, but the claim still fails, and splinting is certainly not optional.

checks.q: A paramedic transfers a patient with an unstable airway to a BLS crew for transport. What has occurred?
choices: A proper transfer of care
Abandonment, because the transfer was to a lower level than the patient needs
Battery
False imprisonment
checks.why: Handing off to a level below what the patient's condition requires ends care improperly, which is abandonment. Battery involves unconsented touching and false imprisonment involves confining someone against their will.

checks.q: An off-duty EMT stops at a crash, provides care within her training in good faith, and accepts no payment. Which is true?
choices: She is fully protected regardless of how she acts
She is generally protected from ordinary negligence claims but not from gross negligence
Good Samaritan laws do not apply to certified providers
She had a legal duty to stop in every state
checks.why: Good Samaritan statutes shield voluntary, good-faith, unpaid care within training from ordinary negligence, with gross negligence carved out. They apply to certified providers acting off duty and do not create a duty to stop.

cards.front: What are the first four things you do when meeting a frightened patient?
cards.back: Say your name and role, ask what they want to be called, ask permission before touching, and get to eye level.

cards.front: Why does fear make patients hard to talk to?
cards.back: Adrenaline shrinks working memory and narrows attention, so complex sentences and stacked questions do not land. Give the brain less to process.

cards.front: How long should you stay silent after asking a patient a question?
cards.back: About five seconds. It feels endless, and it is where the answer the patient was deciding whether to share usually comes out.

cards.front: Name four things you should never promise a patient.
cards.back: That they will be fine, a specific hospital or doctor, a wait time, or that a family member can ride along. Also never give a diagnosis.

cards.front: What is wrong with stacking questions like 'Any pain, nausea, dizziness, or shortness of breath?'
cards.back: A stressed patient answers only the last item or says no to everything. Ask one question, wait for the answer, then ask the next.

cards.front: What can you honestly say instead of 'calm down'?
cards.back: Name the feeling and state your plan: "This is scary. I am going to stay with you and tell you what I am doing as I do it."

cards.front: What is the fastest way to turn an anxious family member into a resource?
cards.back: Give them a concrete job: gather medication bottles, hold the dog, find the insurance card, open the door. Having a task restores the control they lost.

cards.front: How much space should you keep from an escalating person, and how should you stand?
cards.back: At least two arm lengths, roughly 6 feet, angled rather than square on, hands open and visible, with a clear exit for both of you.

cards.front: Why should only one crew member speak during de-escalation?
cards.back: Multiple people reasoning at once reads as an ambush and raises arousal. Pick the person with the best rapport; everyone else stays quiet.

cards.front: How do you respond to a patient describing a delusion?
cards.back: Do not argue and do not agree. Acknowledge the feeling: "I do not see them, but I believe you are scared, and I want to help with that."

cards.front: Which medical causes of agitation must you rule out before calling behavior the problem?
cards.back: Hypoxia, hypoglycemia, head injury, shock, pain, and intoxication. Agitation is a symptom before it is a personality.

cards.front: Why should you get a patient alone in the ambulance when the story does not fit the injuries?
cards.back: A patient who is being controlled or abused cannot disclose in front of the person controlling them. Private time is the only way they can tell you.

cards.front: Who should never serve as an interpreter, and why?
cards.back: Children, always. They lack the vocabulary and should never carry the emotional load. Family members edit, answer for the patient, and may have conflicting interests.

cards.front: What law requires federally funded facilities to provide language access at no cost?
cards.back: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In practice every hospital has a phone or video interpreter line available around the clock.

cards.front: How should you phrase questions when using an interpreter?
cards.back: Speak directly to the patient in the first person, one or two sentences at a time, then pause. Do not say "ask her if..."

cards.front: How do you confirm a patient actually understood through an interpreter?
cards.back: Teach-back: ask the patient to say in their own words what is going to happen. A nod is not comprehension.

cards.front: What does cultural humility mean in practice on a call?
cards.back: Assume you do not know, and ask: about religious items, gender preferences for providers, who makes health decisions in the family, and what the patient thinks is wrong.

cards.front: How long should a radio report be, and what question is it answering?
cards.back: About 30 seconds. The listener is deciding what room, what team, and how fast, so every element should serve that decision.

cards.front: List the elements of a standard radio report in order.
cards.back: Unit and level, receiving facility, ETA, age and sex, chief complaint, level of consciousness, vitals, pertinent history, treatment and response, special requests.

cards.front: What does MIST stand for and when do you use it?
cards.back: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs including vitals, Treatment given. It is the trauma handoff, because mechanism predicts injuries not yet found.

cards.front: What does SBAR stand for?
cards.back: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. It is the standard clinical handoff format inside hospitals.

cards.front: Which element of SBAR is most often omitted and why does that matter?
cards.back: Recommendation. Without stating what you need, the listener has to guess, and nothing happens. "I need you to come look at him" is a valid recommendation.

cards.front: Why should you never use patient names or opinions on the radio?
cards.back: Radio traffic is recorded and may be scanned by the public. Assume any transmission can be played back in court, so state facts plainly and skip commentary.

cards.front: Where and to whom should a handoff be given?
cards.back: At the bedside, to the person actually accepting care, after confirming they are listening, ending with "what questions do you have?"

cards.front: Why is a handoff considered the most dangerous moment in a patient's care?
cards.back: It is the point where information is dropped between teams. Standardized formats such as SBAR and MIST exist specifically to stop those losses.

cards.front: What are the three steps of closed-loop communication?
cards.back: The sender directs a message to a named person, the receiver repeats it back verbatim, and the sender confirms. Then the receiver announces completion with a time.

cards.front: Why is 'someone get the monitor' a communication failure?
cards.back: Diffusion of responsibility: everyone assumes someone else will act. Point at a person, use their name, and give one task.

cards.front: What is the difference between online and offline medical direction?
cards.back: Offline is written protocols and standing orders issued in advance by the medical director. Online is a live radio or phone consult with a physician for orders.

cards.front: What is the two-challenge rule?
cards.back: If you raise a safety concern twice and it is not addressed, you escalate to the next person up the chain. Immediate danger skips straight to escalation.

cards.front: What phrasing makes a junior provider's concern land?
cards.back: Lead with the observation, not the accusation: "I am concerned because his pressure dropped 30 points," then "I am uncomfortable," then "this is a safety issue."

cards.front: What does 'if it is not documented, it was not done' mean in practice?
cards.back: Undocumented care cannot be proven later, so it is treated as never having happened. Documenting care you did not provide is falsification and ends careers.

cards.front: How do you document that a patient seemed intoxicated?
cards.back: Objectively: odor of alcoholic beverage on breath, slurred speech, unsteady gait, plus any direct quote. Never write the conclusion "patient was drunk."

cards.front: Which times must appear in a patient care report?
cards.back: Dispatch, arrival on scene, patient contact, every set of vitals, every intervention including tourniquet application, departure, arrival, and transfer of care.

cards.front: How do you correct an error on a paper PCR?
cards.back: Draw a single line through the error so it stays readable, write the correction next to it, then initial and date. Never erase, scribble out, or use correction fluid.

cards.front: How do you add information remembered after a chart is complete?
cards.back: A late entry, clearly labeled with the date and time it was written. Making an addition look contemporaneous is falsification.

cards.front: Why do you put a patient's subjective statements in quotation marks?
cards.back: A quote is evidence of what was said; your paraphrase is an opinion that can be challenged. Quotes also preserve the patient's own words for the receiving team.

cards.front: Why do pertinent negatives belong in the PCR?
cards.back: They narrow the differential for the receiving clinician and prove you asked. A chart without them looks like the question was never posed.

cards.front: What should a PCR record about each intervention?
cards.back: What was done, the time it was done, who did it, and the patient's response. An intervention without a documented response is half a record.

cards.front: What is the difference between expressed and implied consent?
cards.back: Expressed consent is informed agreement from a patient with capacity. Implied consent covers emergency care for a patient who cannot consent, limited to the emergency.

cards.front: What is the difference between capacity and competence?
cards.back: Competence is a legal status determined by a court. Capacity is your clinical judgment at the bedside about this specific decision at this moment.

cards.front: What four abilities make up decision-making capacity?
cards.back: Understand the information, appreciate how it applies to them, reason through the options, and communicate a consistent choice.

cards.front: Who counts as an emancipated minor?
cards.back: Typically a minor who is married, pregnant or a parent, on active military duty, or declared emancipated by a court. They consent for themselves.

cards.front: What are the seven steps of a proper refusal?
cards.back: Assess fully, determine and document capacity, explain specific risks, offer alternatives, contact medical direction if high risk, obtain a signed and witnessed form, document the conversation with quotes.

cards.front: What are the two types of advance directive recognized in New Jersey?
cards.back: A proxy directive naming a health care representative, and an instruction directive or living will stating what treatment the patient wants. They are often combined.

cards.front: What is POLST and who signs it in New Jersey?
cards.back: Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment, authorized in NJ in 2011. Signed by the patient or representative and by a physician, advanced practice nurse, or physician assistant.

cards.front: What do you do when a DNR form is missing, expired, or contested by family?
cards.back: Begin resuscitation and contact medical direction immediately. You can always stop resuscitation; you cannot recover minutes you did not act.

cards.front: What counts as protected health information?
cards.back: Anything identifying a patient that relates to their health, care, or payment: name, address, date of birth, photos, license plate, room number, or a rare diagnosis locally.

cards.front: What does TPO stand for in HIPAA, and what does it allow?
cards.back: Treatment, Payment, and health care Operations. PHI may be shared for these without specific patient authorization, limited by the minimum necessary standard.

cards.front: Give four everyday actions that are HIPAA breaches.
cards.back: Discussing a patient in a hallway or elevator, looking up a chart that is not yours, photographing a scene or monitor, and posting any identifying detail on social media.

cards.front: What are the HIPAA penalty ranges?
cards.back: Civil penalties run roughly $100 to $50,000 per violation depending on culpability, with annual caps in the millions. Criminal penalties reach 10 years for misuse for gain or malice.

cards.front: In New Jersey, who must report suspected child abuse and to whom?
cards.back: Any person with reasonable cause to believe abuse or neglect occurred, reporting immediately to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. Suspicion is the threshold, not proof.

cards.front: Is 'a police officer asked me' a HIPAA exception?
cards.back: Not by itself. Police get scene and safety information; clinical details generally require patient authorization, a legal mandate such as a gunshot wound report, or a court order.

cards.front: What are the four elements of negligence?
cards.back: Duty, breach of the standard of care, damages, and causation. All four must be proven or the claim fails.

cards.front: What is abandonment?
cards.back: Terminating care without the patient's consent and without transferring to a provider of equal or higher training. Handing a chart to a clerk is the classic example.

cards.front: What is the difference between assault and battery in EMS terms?
cards.back: Assault is placing someone in fear of harmful or offensive contact, such as threatening restraint. Battery is the actual unconsented touching.

cards.front: What is false imprisonment in an EMS context?
cards.back: Confining someone against their will, including transporting a competent adult who has refused, or restraining a patient without lawful basis.

cards.front: What do Good Samaritan laws protect and what do they exclude?
cards.back: They protect voluntary, good-faith, unpaid care within your training from ordinary negligence. They exclude gross negligence, willful misconduct, and on-duty paid care.

cards.front: What is the difference between scope of practice and standard of care?
cards.back: Scope of practice is what your certification legally allows, set by the state, in NJ by the Office of EMS. Standard of care is how a reasonable provider at your level would perform.

quiz.q: You arrive for a 70-year-old man with abdominal pain. Which introduction is most appropriate?
choices: "Sir, I'm Jose, I'm an EMT. May I sit down and ask you a few questions?"
"Hey buddy, what's going on today?"
"We're here for the abdominal pain, lie back please."
"Don't worry, we'll get you fixed right up."
quiz.why: Name, role, and permission at eye level establish trust and consent in one sentence. Diminutives read as condescending to older adults, commands skip consent, and promising a fix is a guarantee you cannot make.

quiz.q: A patient's daughter keeps answering for her alert, oriented mother. What is the best response?
choices: Let the daughter answer since it is faster
Ask the daughter to leave the room immediately
Say you want to hear from the patient first and will come to the daughter next
Address all questions to the daughter and confirm with the patient later
quiz.why: Redirecting keeps a competent patient as the decision maker while preserving the family as a resource. Ejecting the daughter escalates the room, and letting her speak for her mother risks missing coercion or abuse.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old man is pacing, shouting, and clenching his fists in a narrow hallway. What do you do first?
choices: Move closer to show you are not afraid
Position yourself with a clear exit, keep about two arm lengths, and have one crew member speak calmly
Grab his arm to check a pulse and assess for a medical cause
Have both partners explain why he needs to go to the hospital
quiz.why: Space, an exit path, and a single calm voice lower arousal without cornering him. Closing distance and unexpected touch both provoke violence, and multiple speakers feel like being surrounded.

quiz.q: A patient speaks only Mandarin. Her adult son offers to translate and the interpreter line takes three minutes to connect. What is best practice?
choices: Use the son for the entire call to save time
Skip the history and transport
Use the son only briefly for immediate safety information, then switch to the qualified interpreter and document both
Communicate entirely by gestures
quiz.why: Family members edit and may have conflicting interests, so they are a stopgap you document, not a substitute. Skipping the history or relying on gestures leaves you without valid consent or a usable story.

quiz.q: Which statement about using interpreters is correct?
choices: Speak directly to the patient in the first person, pausing every one or two sentences
Speak to the interpreter and let them relay your words
Use precise medical terminology so nothing is lost
Deliver the full explanation at once so the interpreter hears the context
quiz.why: First-person speech directed at the patient keeps her in the conversation and reduces relay errors, and short segments prevent compression. Jargon and long monologues both cause detail loss.

quiz.q: You are transporting a 24-year-old with a gunshot wound to the abdomen. Which handoff format fits best?
choices: SAMPLE
OPQRST
MIST
AVPU
quiz.why: MIST leads with mechanism, which lets the trauma team predict injuries before they examine the patient. SAMPLE and OPQRST are history-gathering tools and AVPU is a single mental status measure.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest SBAR recommendation from an ED tech?
choices: "I just wanted to let you know about room 4."
"His pressure is 84/50 and he looks worse than 20 minutes ago. I need you to come see him now."
"Something seems off with the guy in 4."
"I'll check on him again in a while."
quiz.why: A specific finding plus a direct request for action is what produces a response. Vague statements and deferred rechecks leave the nurse without a reason to move, which is exactly how deterioration is missed.

quiz.q: Which item does NOT belong in a 30-second radio report?
choices: Estimated time of arrival
Chief complaint and level of consciousness
The patient's full name and address
Treatment given and the response
quiz.why: Identifying details are unnecessary for the receiving team's preparation and put PHI over an unsecured, recorded channel. ETA, complaint, mental status, and treatment response all directly shape room and team assignment.

quiz.q: You are in a busy ED and no nurse is available to take your stable patient. What should you do?
choices: Hand the PCR to the unit secretary and clear
Leave the patient in a hallway bed and notify the charge nurse by text
Stay with the patient until a nurse accepts care at the bedside
Return the patient to the ambulance and wait outside
quiz.why: Care continues until a provider of equal or higher training accepts it, so remaining with the patient is the only option that avoids abandonment. A secretary cannot accept clinical care and a text is not a transfer.

quiz.q: A paramedic hands you a syringe and says 'give this.' What is the correct action?
choices: Ask him to state the drug, dose, and route, repeat it back, and confirm before giving
Give it, since the paramedic is senior to you
Hand it to the patient's family to hold
Set it down and say nothing
quiz.why: Closed-loop communication with an explicit drug, dose, and route catches errors before they reach the patient, and an unlabeled syringe is never safe to administer. Seniority does not substitute for verification.

quiz.q: Which is an example of online medical direction?
choices: A protocol book allowing oxygen for hypoxia
A standing order for oral glucose in a conscious hypoglycemic patient
Radioing the emergency physician for permission on a high-risk refusal
A regional treatment guideline published annually
quiz.why: Online direction is live contact with a physician during the call. Protocols, standing orders, and published guidelines are all issued in advance, which makes them offline direction.

quiz.q: You tell a nurse twice that a patient's oxygen saturation has fallen to 86 percent and nothing changes. What is your next step?
choices: Wait and recheck in ten minutes
Escalate to the charge nurse or physician
Document your concern and move on
Adjust the treatment yourself outside your scope
quiz.why: The two-challenge rule says two unaddressed attempts means escalating up the chain. Waiting or documenting alone leaves a hypoxic patient untreated, and acting outside your scope creates a second problem.

quiz.q: Which PCR narrative entry is written correctly?
choices: Patient was being dramatic about the pain
Patient probably has a kidney stone
Patient seemed fine overall
Patient rated pain 8 of 10, stated "it feels like someone is sitting on me," no radiation reported
quiz.why: A measured severity, a direct quote, and a pertinent negative are objective and defensible. Judgments about a patient's behavior, field diagnoses, and vague impressions are all conclusions rather than findings.

quiz.q: Two days after a call you realize you documented the wrong medication name in an electronic PCR. What is correct?
choices: Use the system's amendment function to add a dated correction
Edit the original text so the record reads correctly
Ask your supervisor to delete the report
Leave it, since the record is closed
quiz.why: Electronic records keep an audit trail, so an amendment is both the honest and the only defensible path. Silent editing and deletion look like concealment, and leaving a known error unaddressed is clinically unsafe.

quiz.q: Why are times recorded for every intervention on the PCR?
choices: Insurance requires only the transport time
It makes the report longer
Times are optional if the narrative is thorough
Timing establishes the sequence and duration of care, which is often the central question later
quiz.why: How long something took, and in what order, is frequently the entire question in a quality review or a lawsuit, and tourniquet time directly changes clinical decisions. Times are never optional.

quiz.q: An unconscious 30-year-old is pulled from a crash with no family present. Under what principle do you treat?
choices: Expressed consent
Implied consent
Involuntary consent
You may not treat without authorization
quiz.why: Implied consent assumes a reasonable person would want lifesaving care when they cannot consent themselves. Expressed consent requires the patient to agree, and involuntary consent involves legal authority such as a police hold.

quiz.q: A 35-year-old with a blood glucose of 44 mg/dL is alert and oriented times four and wants to refuse. What is true?
choices: He may refuse because he is oriented
You must call police to force transport
Have him sign a refusal and leave
He lacks capacity because hypoglycemia impairs judgment; treat under implied consent
quiz.why: Orientation is not capacity, and a glucose of 44 mg/dL impairs the reasoning needed for an informed decision. Treating the hypoglycemia often restores capacity, after which the decision can be revisited.

quiz.q: Which statement about a valid DNR order is correct?
choices: It applies only to resuscitation attempts in cardiac arrest, and comfort care continues
It means withhold all treatment including oxygen
It expires when the patient leaves a hospital
It can be overridden by any family member at the scene
quiz.why: A DNR limits resuscitation, not care, so oxygen, positioning, bleeding control, and comfort all continue. A portable order such as POLST is designed to travel between settings, and family objection prompts medical direction contact rather than automatic override.

quiz.q: Who may sign a New Jersey POLST form alongside the patient or their representative?
choices: Any registered nurse
The EMT on scene
A hospital social worker
A physician, advanced practice nurse, or physician assistant
quiz.why: POLST is a medical order, so it requires a clinician with prescriptive authority: a physician, APN, or PA. Nurses, social workers, and EMTs may help complete or honor the form but cannot sign it as the ordering clinician.

quiz.q: Which action is a HIPAA violation?
choices: Giving the receiving physician the patient's medication list
Reporting a gunshot wound as required by state law
Looking up your neighbor's chart because you saw the ambulance at her house
Sharing the run data with your service's quality improvement review
quiz.why: Curiosity is not treatment, payment, or operations, and audit logs catch chart lookups reliably. Handing off to the treating physician, legally mandated reporting, and internal QI review are all permitted uses.

quiz.q: You post on social media about an unusual call, with no name, but you mention the street and the type of injury. Is this a breach?
choices: No, because you omitted the name
Yes, because the details could identify the patient in that community
No, because you deleted it an hour later
Only if the patient sees the post
quiz.why: PHI includes any combination of details that reasonably identifies someone, and location plus a distinctive injury does exactly that. Deleting a post does not undo a disclosure, and a breach does not require the patient to notice.

quiz.q: You see bruises in varying stages of healing on a 4-year-old and the story keeps changing. What is your obligation in New Jersey?
choices: Report immediately to the State Central Registry and notify the receiving facility, documenting objective findings
Confront the caregiver on scene for an explanation
Wait until a physician confirms abuse
Report only if the child says someone hurt her
quiz.why: New Jersey requires any person with reasonable cause to report immediately; suspicion, not proof, is the threshold, and reporting in good faith is protected. Confronting a caregiver can endanger the child and destroy the investigation.

quiz.q: A police officer at a crash asks you for the patient's medical history 'for the report.' What is the correct response?
choices: Provide the full history since police are on scene
Refuse to speak to police at all
Provide the history only if the officer signs your PCR
Provide scene and safety information, and refer clinical requests to your supervisor or through proper legal channels
quiz.why: Law enforcement presence is not itself a HIPAA exception; clinical details generally require authorization, a legal mandate, or a court order. Refusing all cooperation is also wrong, since scene and safety information is appropriate to share.

quiz.q: An EMT starts an assessment on a competent adult who has clearly said no. What has occurred?
choices: Assault only
Battery
Abandonment
Negligence, automatically
quiz.why: Battery is the unconsented touching itself; assault would be the threat of contact without the touching. Abandonment involves ending care improperly, and negligence still requires proof of harm and causation.

quiz.q: Which scenario establishes all four elements of negligence?
choices: A dispatched EMT fails to immobilize a spinal injury and the patient develops new paralysis during transport
An EMT is rude but provides correct care
An off-duty EMT drives past a crash in a state with no duty to stop
An EMT performs a skill correctly that the patient later regrets consenting to
quiz.why: That case has duty from dispatch, breach of the standard, real damages in the new deficit, and causation linking the two. Rudeness causes no harm, no duty exists in the drive-by, and a correctly performed consented skill breaches nothing.

quiz.q: Which best describes abandonment?
choices: Transporting a patient to a hospital they did not choose
Terminating care without transferring to a provider of equal or higher training
Refusing to transport a patient who has no insurance
Failing to obtain a full set of vital signs
quiz.why: Abandonment is specifically the improper termination of an established care relationship. Hospital choice disputes, insurance discrimination, and incomplete assessment are all problems, but they are different legal and ethical failures.

quiz.q: An off-duty EMT stops at a crash and, without training or equipment for it, attempts a procedure far outside her scope, worsening the injury. Does the Good Samaritan law protect her?
choices: Yes, because she volunteered in good faith
Yes, because she accepted no payment
Yes, because off-duty providers are always immune
Likely not, because acting far outside her training may be gross negligence
quiz.why: Good Samaritan protection applies to good-faith care within the responder's training and does not extend to gross negligence or willful misconduct. Volunteering and declining payment do not immunize conduct that is reckless.

quiz.q: A competent adult refuses transport after a low-speed crash. Which single omission most weakens your documentation?
choices: Not recording the weather
Not listing the police unit number
Not recording your partner's certification number
Not documenting the specific risks explained and the patient's understanding of them
quiz.why: Informed refusal rests on proof the patient was told what could happen and could restate it, so that conversation is the core of the record. Weather, unit numbers, and certification numbers are administrative details that do not establish informed refusal.

scenarios.title: The refusal: 61-year-old who fell off a ladder
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched at 1615 to a residence for a fall. A 61-year-old man fell about 8 feet off a ladder while cleaning gutters, landing on grass. His wife called 911. He is standing in the driveway when you arrive and tells you before you are out of the ambulance that he does not need to go anywhere. He takes apixaban, a blood thinner, for atrial fibrillation.

steps.prompt:
He is walking, talking in full sentences, and mildly annoyed that his wife called.

"I'm fine. I just want you guys to leave."

What do you do first?

choices.text: Hand him the refusal form to sign so he can get on with his day
choices.feedback: You cannot document a refusal on a patient you never assessed. A signature obtained before an assessment and a risks conversation is close to worthless.

choices.text: Ask permission to assess him, explaining you need to check a few things before anyone signs anything
choices.feedback: Correct. The refusal sequence starts with a complete assessment. Asking permission also keeps him in control, which is usually what the annoyance is about.

choices.text: Tell him he has to go because he is on a blood thinner
choices.feedback: The clinical concern is right but the framing is wrong. Telling a competent adult he has no choice invites a fight and, if you transported him against his will, would be false imprisonment.

steps.prompt:
He agrees to be checked. Assessment: alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event. No loss of consciousness reported and his wife confirms he never lost consciousness. Small abrasion on the left forearm. Mild tenderness over the left lower ribs. No neck or back pain. No headache. Glucose 104. Breath smells of nothing unusual.

What is the next step in the refusal sequence?

choices.text: Determine and document decision-making capacity with specific evidence
choices.feedback: Correct. Orientation is only part of it. Capacity means he can understand, appreciate, reason, and communicate a consistent choice, and you write down what showed you that.

choices.text: Note that he is alert and oriented times four, which settles capacity
choices.feedback: Common error. Orientation and capacity are not the same thing. A patient can score four out of four and still be unable to reason through a specific decision.

choices.text: Call medical direction before anything else
choices.feedback: Medical direction is a step in this sequence, but not yet. Establish capacity and give the risks first so the physician has something to work with.

choices.text: Document that he seems fine and move to the signature
choices.feedback: "Seems fine" is a conclusion, not documentation, and skips both the capacity determination and the risks conversation, which are the two parts that matter later.

steps.prompt:
He can explain that he fell, that you are concerned about bleeding, and that he is choosing to stay home. He is consistent about it.
