Now you explain the risks. Which version is correct?

choices.text: "You should really go, it's better to be safe than sorry."
choices.feedback: Too vague to count. A risks conversation must name the specific consequence, and this could describe a stubbed toe as easily as a head bleed.

choices.text: "Because you take apixaban, a fall like this can cause bleeding inside your head or your chest that may not show symptoms for hours. That bleeding can cause permanent injury or kill you, and the only way to rule it out is a scan."
choices.feedback: Correct. Specific mechanism, specific consequence including death, and the reason transport is the only way to answer the question. This is what informed refusal looks like.

choices.text: "If you don't come with us, you could die, and that's on you."
choices.feedback: The content is technically true but the delivery is coercive and unprofessional, and it usually hardens the refusal. Blame does not inform anyone.

steps.prompt:
He listens, then says: "I hear you. I still don't want to go. My daughter's a nurse, she's coming over tonight."

What do you do now?

choices.text: Ask him to repeat the risks back in his own words, offer alternatives, and contact online medical direction
choices.feedback: Correct, and all three matter. Teach-back proves understanding, alternatives such as calling back or seeing his doctor today keep the door open, and a high-risk refusal on an anticoagulated head-injury patient warrants a physician.

choices.text: Accept the refusal and get the signature, since he clearly understood
choices.feedback: You skipped the two things that make this defensible: teach-back and medical direction. Anticoagulation plus a head-height fall is a high-risk refusal.

choices.text: Tell him his daughter being a nurse is not good enough and keep arguing
choices.feedback: Arguing rarely changes a decision and often ends the conversation early. Acknowledge the plan, then give him the specific warning signs and the alternatives.

choices.text: Have his wife sign the refusal on his behalf
choices.feedback: A spouse cannot consent or refuse for a competent adult. The form has to be his, and using hers would misrepresent the record.

steps.prompt:
Medical direction speaks with him by phone and agrees he has capacity. He still refuses. His wife is willing to stay with him overnight.

What completes the call?

choices.text: Signature from the patient, a witness signature, specific return precautions given out loud and in writing, and a narrative with quotes
choices.feedback: Correct. Return precautions for an anticoagulated head injury include new headache, vomiting, confusion, sleepiness, weakness, or any change, and you tell them to call 911 immediately rather than drive.

choices.text: Signature only, since the physician cleared it
choices.feedback: The physician consult is one element, not a replacement for the rest. A witness and documented return precautions are what show the whole process happened.

choices.text: Skip the form since medical direction approved verbally
choices.feedback: A verbal physician agreement with no signed form leaves no record that the patient was informed and chose. If it is not documented, it was not done.

steps.prompt: You are writing the narrative. Which entry is written correctly?

choices.text: "Pt refused. Was A&O x4. Seemed to understand. Signed refusal."
choices.feedback: Almost all conclusions and no evidence. It does not record the risks explained, the teach-back, the physician contact, or the alternatives offered.

choices.text: "Pt alert, oriented x4, glucose 104, no evidence of intoxication or head injury on exam. Risks of intracranial and intrathoracic bleeding on apixaban explained, including permanent injury and death. Pt restated risk in own words: \"I could have a bleed in my head and not know it.\" Alternatives offered. Dr. Patel contacted 1642, agreed pt has capacity. Return precautions given verbally and in writing. Refusal signed by pt, witnessed by spouse 1648."
choices.feedback: Correct. Objective findings, the specific risks, the patient's own words as evidence of understanding, the physician by name and time, alternatives, precautions, and a witnessed signature with a time.

choices.text: "Pt is a stubborn guy who didn't want to listen. Told him he was making a mistake."
choices.feedback: Editorializing about a patient in a legal document damages you, not him. Record behavior and quotes, never character judgments.

scenarios.debrief: A refusal is the highest-risk call an EMT runs, because nothing appears to go wrong until hours later. The sequence that protects the patient and you is fixed: assess fully, determine and document capacity with evidence, explain the specific risks including death where real, confirm understanding with teach-back in the patient's own words, offer alternatives, contact medical direction for any high-risk refusal, and obtain a signed and witnessed form with documented return precautions. Two traps live in this case. Alert and oriented times four is not capacity, and anticoagulation converts an ordinary fall into a high-risk one, because a subdural bleed on apixaban can be silent for hours. Notice also what you never do: sign for the patient, let a spouse sign for a competent adult, transport against a valid refusal, or write your opinion of the patient into the chart.

scenarios.title: Handoff: giving SBAR in a full department
scenarios.intro: You are working as an emergency department technician. At 1930 you are asked to move a 68-year-old woman from triage to bed 9. She came in for weakness and a cough for three days. As you settle her in you get a set of vitals and notice she looks worse than her triage note suggests. The department is full, the nurse assigned to bed 9 is in another room, and the physician is at the workstation.

steps.prompt:
Vitals you just obtained in bed 9. Triage 40 minutes ago recorded HR 96, BP 124/76, RR 20, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temp 38.1 C.

What do you do first?

choices.text: Chart the vitals and continue with your assigned tasks
choices.feedback: Charting alone does not move anyone. A falling pressure with a rising heart rate, rising temperature, and dropping saturation over 40 minutes is a deteriorating patient who needs someone at the bedside now.

choices.text: Recheck the blood pressure manually, place her on continuous monitoring and oxygen per protocol, and find the assigned nurse immediately
choices.feedback: Correct. Confirm the abnormal number, do what is in your scope, and escalate at once. A single automated reading is worth confirming, but not worth waiting on.

choices.text: Wait for the nurse to come to the room on her own
choices.feedback: In a full department that could be twenty minutes. This trend is the early phase of septic shock and the clock matters.

choices.text: Tell the patient to let you know if she feels worse and step out
choices.feedback: Delegating the monitoring to a hypoxic, febrile 68-year-old is not monitoring. She may not recognize her own decline.

steps.prompt:
You find the nurse in the hallway between rooms.

How do you open?

choices.text: "When you get a chance, bed 9's numbers changed a little."
choices.feedback: Hedged and vague. "A little" and "when you get a chance" both tell her this can wait, which is the opposite of the message.

choices.text: "Sarah, I need 30 seconds. Bed 9 is deteriorating and I'm concerned."
choices.feedback: Correct. Her name, an explicit time request, the headline first, and the word concerned, which is the standard signal that this is a safety issue.

choices.text: "Sorry to bother you, I know you're busy, it's probably nothing, but..."
choices.feedback: Apologizing and pre-discounting your own concern buries the message. You are not bothering anyone; you are reporting a deteriorating patient.

steps.prompt:
She stops and gives you her attention.

Give the S and B of your SBAR.

choices.text: "She came in for weakness. She's 68. I think she might be septic, we should probably start fluids and get a lactate."
choices.feedback: You jumped to recommendation before giving the data, and as a tech you are not making the diagnosis. Give the situation and the background first; your read belongs in A, framed as observation.

choices.text: "Situation: bed 9, Mrs. Okoye, 68, in for three days of cough and weakness, now looking worse than at triage. Background: triage at 1850 had her at HR 96, BP 124/76, temp 38.1, sat 96 on room air."
choices.feedback: Correct. Who, what, and the baseline the listener needs so your next numbers mean something. The comparison is the whole point of the background.

choices.text: "She's a 68-year-old with a history of hypertension, diabetes, a hysterectomy in 2004, and she lives with her daughter who says she's been tired since Tuesday."
choices.feedback: Too much background and no situation. An old surgical history does not help the nurse decide whether to walk into that room right now.

steps.prompt:
Now the A and the R.

Which is correct for your role?

choices.text: "Assessment: repeat vitals at 1930 are HR 118, BP 96/58, RR 26, sat 91 on room air, temp 38.9. She's warm, breathing faster, and answering more slowly than she was in triage. Recommendation: I put her on the monitor and oxygen, and I need you to come see her now."
choices.feedback: Correct. Objective numbers with the trend, your observations rather than a diagnosis, what you already did, and an explicit request for action with a time frame.

choices.text: "Assessment: she's septic. Recommendation: start two large-bore IVs, give 30 mL/kg of fluid, and draw blood cultures."
choices.feedback: Those may all be correct clinically and none of them are yours to order. Stating a diagnosis and a treatment plan outside your scope undermines the report and your credibility.

choices.text: "Assessment: she doesn't look good. Recommendation: maybe check on her at some point."
choices.feedback: No data and no actionable request. "Doesn't look good" is an impression that cannot be prioritized against the other twelve patients in the department.

choices.text: "Assessment: her numbers are all off. Recommendation: I'll keep watching her."
choices.feedback: Vague on the data and the recommendation moves the responsibility back to you. Your job is to hand the concern to someone who can act on it.

steps.prompt:
The nurse says she will be there in two minutes and asks you to repeat the pressure. She then says to the physician, "Bed 9 is 96 over 58, was 124 over 76 forty minutes ago, febrile and hypoxic."

The physician says "Get me a lactate and a 12-lead." The nurse turns to you.

What is the correct response?

choices.text: Nod and go do it
choices.feedback: The tasks may be right but the loop is open. If you misheard one of them, nobody finds out until the wrong test comes back.

choices.text: "Lactate and a 12-lead on bed 9, copy. I'll tell you when the 12-lead is on the machine."
choices.feedback: Correct. Repeat back the orders and commit to announcing completion. That is a closed loop, and it takes three seconds.

choices.text: "Someone should probably get those."
choices.feedback: Diffusion of responsibility. A task assigned to no one in particular is a task nobody does, which is exactly what closed-loop communication exists to prevent.

steps.prompt:
The patient's son arrives, upset, and asks you in the hallway what is wrong with his mother and whether she is going to be okay. He also asks you to take a photo of the monitor so he can send it to his sister, a nurse in another state.

How do you respond?

choices.text: Tell him the team is working on her, walk him to the room, and let him hear from the nurse or physician; decline the photo and explain the department's policy
choices.feedback: Correct. You acknowledge him, connect him to the person who can answer, and decline the photo. Photographing a monitor and sending it out is a PHI disclosure regardless of family relationship.

choices.text: Tell him she has sepsis and is very sick
choices.feedback: That is a diagnosis, it is not yours to give, and it may be wrong. Techs relay that the team is working and connect families to the clinician.

choices.text: Take the photo, since the sister is a nurse and it is his own mother
choices.feedback: Being a family member or a nurse elsewhere does not make someone part of this patient's care team. This is a breach, and phone photos in clinical areas are prohibited almost everywhere.

choices.text: Tell him "she's going to be fine, don't worry" so he calms down
choices.feedback: Never promise an outcome. If she deteriorates, that sentence is the one the family remembers and repeats, and it destroys trust in the whole team.

scenarios.debrief: This is the handoff pattern you will use every shift. Confirm the abnormal number, do what is in your scope, then escalate by name with the headline first. SBAR makes the escalation usable: situation says who and what, background gives the baseline that makes your numbers mean something, assessment gives objective findings and your observations, and recommendation states what you need. As a technician your recommendation is a request, not an order, and "I need you to come see her now" is both appropriate and powerful. Three habits carried the call. Naming the person you are speaking to, refusing to soften the message with apologies and hedges, and closing the loop by repeating orders back and announcing completion. The family interaction is the other half of the job: acknowledge, connect them to the clinician who can answer, never diagnose, never promise an outcome, and never let PHI leave the department on a phone.
